title: Looking Skyward

paragraphs.text: From the moment the first hot-air balloon took flight in France in 1783, the earliest pioneers of human flight believed that the true future of aviation depended on lighter-than-air inflatables and the creation of massive airships. Witnessing that event, US scientist and senior statesman Benjamin Franklin believed hot-air balloons to be ‘a discovery of great importance’, and even suggested that they may bring an end to conflict between countries. By the late 19th century, balloons had been used for sport, travel, commerce, adventure, and, despite Franklin’s dreams, even war. But these designs were largely similar to the balloon-and-basket we are still familiar with today. Then, when the Wright Brothers took to the air with their 1903 aeroplane, plans for balloon travel were largely abandoned. There was still a recreational use for balloons, and dreams of airships never quite died, but with the dawn of the 20th century, scientists, designers and engineers seem to have switched their attentions to mastering the aeroplane.

But while the golden age of hot-air balloons and airships still existed, there were a few inventors who designed incredibly complex balloon machines. One of the largest airships imagined by early balloonists was proposed by a physicist named Robertson in 1804. He announced to the public that it would be supported by a 150-foot diameter balloon and designed to carry up to 150,000 pounds. For its first voyage, Robertson planned for it to carry 60 people, mostly academics, halfway around the world to observe, collect data, and conduct experiments. The great ship that carried these important passengers would be equipped with ‘all the things necessary for the convenience, the observations, and even the pleasures of the voyagers’. However, Robertson’s plans were never realised.

Of course, he wasn’t alone in his dreams of mastering the skies for economic and cultural gain. French balloonist Jusque La Petin designed a 160-yard-long airship held up by four enormous balloons. Unlike some of the other designs, there was no primary cabin for passengers, but rather an enormous platform. Petin asked the French government for financial assistance but they would have none of it. Their reluctance may be explained by what some reported as a fear that ballooning would encourage smuggling and destabilize the country. Another innovation was the ‘saddle balloon’, conceived by German engineer George Rodek around 1895, which was designed to lift a single person in a kind of harness below, with meteorological instruments and sandbags attached. In the only surviving illustration of this invention, we can see Rodek himself, who actually built this device and amazed everyone watching by taking off in his incredible, though surely uncomfortable, vehicle.

Irishman Richard Crosbie was one inventor and balloonist whose fame has lasted. When he read newspaper reports about earlier ballooning successes in France, he decided to carry out some experiments of his own. He wisely chose hydrogen rather than hot air to create lift in his balloons. This was a safer option, and eliminated the risks involved in using straw or sheep's wool to create fire. Made of rubber on the inside, the balloon he eventually designed was enclosed in silk, and was 40 feet in diameter. He called the ‘basket’ that would be attached to it the ‘Aeronautic Chariot’, which combined the design of a ship with its masts, sails, paddles, and rigging, with the more traditional basket design. It was spacious enough to carry not just passengers, but also the equipment required for checking wind and weather conditions. In order to raise the funds needed to see the project through to completion, Crosbie was obliged to exhibit the Aeronautic Chariot to the public for a period of time, charging a small fee.

Then came the time for the test flight. On the final day of his exhibition, he launched the balloon skywards. It travelled north-west, rolled up the Scottish coast and was successfully picked up, together with the cat that had been travelling in the basket, near the Isle of Man the following day. Crosbie let his fans know that next time he would be on board, and would be crossing the Irish sea. On 19 July 1785, he stepped into his aeronautical chariot, defying a ban by the Mayor of Dublin on balloon flights because the population of the city was spending long periods staring at the sky instead of working. He saluted the 20,000 strong crowd, ordered the ropes cut, and rose into the heavens over Dublin. He was visible for three and a half minutes, then disappeared into a cloud. His audience roared with delight. As it happened, he came down halfway across the Irish sea due to a severe storm, and had to be picked up by a passing ship. Nevertheless, the flight was hailed across Europe as a ploneering scientific achievement and considered a great victory for Ireland.

Today, with a few notable exceptions, the hot-air balloon that once seemed poised to change the world is mostly just used for sightseeing and wedding proposals, but the inventiveness of those early designs will always inspire wonder at what could have been.
